extracted.intended_audience: manufacturing managers, bridge contractors, and industrial entrepreneurs (construction/iron & steel industry)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical standards and business rules-of-thumb for 19th-century iron/steel manufacture and bridge construction: material selection, quality control, accounting, customer negotiation, and shop discipline that together determine successful contracts and durable structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use only the best material and enough of it; make our own iron and steel
rubrics_metrics.description: We used only the best material and enough of it, making our own iron and later our own steel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keystone bridges 'don't fall' because of superior material and sufficient quantity; controlling raw-material production ensured uniform quality and availability when others might skimp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be our own severest inspectors; build a safe structure or none at all
rubrics_metrics.description: We were our own severest inspectors, and would build a safe structure or none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asked to build a bridge known to be of insufficient strength or unscientific design, the firm resolutely declined. This internal insistence on safety and refusal to accept unsafe specifications underpins reputation and long-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcome external inspectors; treat inspection as a benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of objecting to inspectors they should be welcomed by all manufacturing establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Welcoming inspectors helps maintain a high standard, educates workers to reach excellence, and contrasts with firms that chased away inspectors and later failed under competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clean, well-equipped workshops and yards
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean, fine workshops and tools, well-kept yards and surroundings are of much greater importance than is usually supposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good physical environment improves workmanship and morale; it's an underestimated factor in achieving consistent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put quality before price; quality is the foundation of business success
rubrics_metrics.description: The surest foundation of a manufacturing concern is quality. After that, and a long way after, comes cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High quality may mean uphill work at first, but once proven it leads to smooth sailing. Long-term reputation and reliability outweigh short-term price competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be on the spot when contracts are let and secure written agreements in person
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want a contract, be on the spot when it is let. And if possible stay on hand until you can take the written contract home in your pocket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: presence at Dubuque (and the cast-iron lamp-post example) helped secure a major contract; being physically present can capture unexpected opportunities and prevent losing awards to rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand material properties and choose appropriate materials (wrought vs cast iron)
rubrics_metrics.description: We had always made the upper cord of the bridge of wrought-iron, while our rivals' was made of cast-iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technical arguments and practical analogies (e.g., a cast-iron lamp-post broke on impact while wrought-iron would bend) to persuade non-technical decision-makers; critical members should avoid brittle materials like cast iron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce precise accounting and weighing systems to know costs and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce such a system of weighing and accounting as would enable us to know what our cost was for each process and especially what each man was doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move away from 'lump business' practices; weigh materials at points in the mill, track processes and individual output to detect waste, reward productivity, and hold people accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt improved technology even if initially criticized when it reduces waste
rubrics_metrics.description: The Siemens Gas Furnace had been used to some extent in Great Britain ... in the heating of great masses of material, almost half the waste could sometimes be saved by using the new furnaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in efficient processes (even at apparent extra expense) because long-term savings and product quality justify the cost; anticipate initial skepticism from established practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate customers and settle disputes fairly to maintain relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: We always accommodated our customers, even although at some expense to ourselves, and in cases of dispute we gave the other party the benefit of the doubt and settled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lawsuits and maintain goodwill; fair treatment fosters long-term business and reputational advantages (examples: sustained relationships with important railroads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to share intellectual property or accept less immediate return for strategic endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: He asked me if we would permit him to use our patents. I replied that we would feel highly honored by the Baltimore and Ohio doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing a major customer to use patents (or giving public endorsement) can be worth far more than patent fees because it secures reputational value and future contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage contractual risk with clear arrangements and practical mitigations
rubrics_metrics.description: I offered my personal bond to guarantee opening bridges on time; we later relieved ourselves from all responsibility upon the bond by placing the superstructure on the banks awaiting the completion of the substructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate bonds/guarantees when necessary but design project sequencing and logistics (e.g., pre-fabricating superstructure) to limit exposure and meet deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take on difficult, unusual, or bespoke work that others avoid, provided quality is assured
rubrics_metrics.description: We began at the new mill by making all shapes which were required, and especially such as no other concern would undertake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filling niche technical needs builds business advantage; specialize in items others cannot produce, while maintaining strict quality standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire, promote, and trust capable, thorough mechanics and clerks; reward initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce thorough mechanics and clerks; those who developed novel systems of accounting or machines were promoted and made partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kloman's mechanical inventions and Borntraeger's accounting statement led to promotion and partnership; encourage and recognize internal innovation and initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse to build 'cheap' unsafe structures; do not compromise safety for profit
rubrics_metrics.description: We never have built and we never will build a cheap bridge. Ours don't fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize long-term safety and reputation; short-term cheaper bids that compromise safety risk disaster and ruin reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tactful technical persuasion to educate non-expert decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: When directors were 'delightfully ignorant' of merits of cast- and wrought-iron, use clear illustrations and advocates to demonstrate the practical difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain technical risks in familiar terms and enlist credible witnesses (an engineer or a respected local) to influence boards who may lack technical knowledge.
